```{r, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
format_p <- function(x) format.pval(x, digits = 4, eps = 0)
```

## ARIMA vs. ETS

### 2.1. Monthly liquor store sales

**2.1a** I looked at monthly U.S. sales at beer, wine, and liquor stores from January 1992 through December 2019. The sales numbers are in millions of dollars and haven’t been adjusted for seasonality. Every month is accounted for, giving a complete set of 336 months. I stopped the sample at the end of 2019 to avoid the wild swings during the pandemic. [FRED series](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MRTSSM4453USN)

```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv", na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(
    Month = yearmonth(observation_date),
    sales = MRTSSM4453USN
  ) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(
    Month >= yearmonth("1992 Jan"),
    Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec")
  )

has_gaps(liquor)
```

```{r}
autoplot(liquor, sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. beer, wine, and liquor store sales",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Sales (millions of dollars)"
  )
```

```{r}
gg_season(
  liquor, log(sales),
  pal = gray.colors(9, start = 0.68, end = 0.12)
) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal pattern in log liquor store sales",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Log sales",
    colour = "Year"
  )
```

**2.1b** Sales usually go up over time. December generally stands out as the big peak, and then things drop off sharply in January and February. There’s also a smaller bump in late spring and summer. The December spike gets bigger in dollar terms as sales grow, suggesting that the seasonal swings are proportional to the level of sales. Taking logs helps stabilize those swings across years.

### 2.2. Model selection and residuals

```{r}
liquor_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_fit.rds")

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

**2.2a** The automatically selected ARIMA model was **ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)[12] with drift**. It uses one seasonal difference, so it subtracts log sales from the same month a year before. There are no ordinary differences. The automatically selected ETS model was ETS(A,A,A), which means it uses additive errors, an additive trend, and additive seasonality on the log scale.

```{r, fig.height=6.4}
liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
diag_arima <- readRDS("results/liquor_diagnostics.rds")

diag_arima$ljung_box |>
  transmute(
    Lag = 24L,
    `AR and MA terms` = diag_arima$dof,
    `Test df` = 24L - diag_arima$dof,
    `Ljung–Box Q` = lb_stat,
    `p-value` = format_p(lb_pvalue)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**2.2b** There were six estimated AR and MA coefficients, $1+2+2+1=6$. With 24 lags, the Ljung–Box test ends up with 18 degrees of freedom. The residuals bounce around zero, but a few autocorrelations go past the reference lines. The test statistic was **120.39**, with $p \approx 3.54\times10^{-17}$. So, there’s still some serial correlation in the residuals. That’s why I’d look at how the model does on months it hasn’t seen yet.

### 2.3. Expanding-window forecast comparison

**2.3a** I started with a training window from January 1992 through December 2001. I kept the starting date fixed and added one month to the training sample at each step. This gave me **216 forecast origins**, from December 2001 through November 2019.

```{r}
liquor_accuracy <- readRDS("results/liquor_accuracy.rds")

liquor_accuracy |>
  select(Model = .model, RMSE, MAE) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    caption = "One-month sales forecast errors in millions of dollars"
  )
```

**2.3b** The first forecast I made was for **January 2002**, and the last was for **December 2019**. Both RMSE and MAE ranked ARIMA first, ETS second, and the seasonal random walk third. ARIMA’s **average absolute forecast error was $65.65 million** per month.

### 2.4. Equal-accuracy tests

```{r}
liquor_dm <- readRDS("results/liquor_dm.rds")

liquor_dm |>
  transmute(
    Comparison,
    DM,
    `p-value` = format_p(p_value)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**2.4** When I compared ARIMA and ETS, the Diebold–Mariano statistic came out to **−2.906** with $p=0.00404$. Comparing ARIMA to the seasonal random walk gave **−10.755** with $p\approx7.28\times10^{-22}$. Both tests reject equal expected squared error at the 5% level, favoring ARIMA. So, if I had to plan next month’s inventory, I’d go with ARIMA.
